<fragment>

Tupelo has a deep connection to Mississippi's music history, being known as the birthplace of Elvis Presley and Diplo as well as the origin of the group Rae Sremmurd. The city is home to multiple art and cultural institutions, including the Elvis Presley Birthplace and the 10,000-seat Cadence Bank Arena, the largest multipurpose indoor arena in Mississippi. Tupelo is the only city in the Southern United States to be named an All-America City five times, most recently in 2015.[10] Its Main Street program, Downtown Tupelo Main Street Association, was the winner of the national Main Street's Great American Main Street Award in 2020.


The Tupelo micropolitan area contains Lee, Itawamba, and Pontotoc counties and had a population of 140,081 in 2017.[11]

Some of the songs, like "That's All Right", were in what one Memphis journalist described as the "R&B idiom of negro field jazz"; others, like "Blue Moon of Kentucky", were "more in the country field", "but there was a curious blending of the two different musics in both".[72] This blend of styles made it difficult for Presley's music to find radio airplay. According to Neal, many country-music disc jockeys would not play it because Presley sounded too much like a black artist and none of the R&B stations would touch him because "he sounded too much like a hillbilly."[73] The blend came to be known as "rockabilly". At the time, Presley was variously billed as "The King of Western Bop", "The Hillbilly Cat", and "The Memphis Flash".[74]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Presley, who received no formal music training and could not read music, studied and played by ear. He also visited record stores that provided jukeboxes and listening booths to customers. He knew all of Hank Snow's songs,[30] and he loved records by other country singers such as Roy Acuff, Ernest Tubb, Ted Daffan, Jimmie Rodgers, Jimmie Davis, and Bob Wills.[31] The Southern gospel singer Jake Hess, one of his favorite performers, was a significant influence on his ballad-singing style.[32][33] Presley was a regular audience member at the monthly All-Night Singings downtown, where many of the white gospel groups that performed reflected the influence of African American spiritual music.[34] He adored the music of black gospel singer Sister Rosetta Tharpe.[31]


</fragment>
<fragment>

Presley listened to regional radio stations, such as WDIA, that played what were then called "race records": spirituals, blues, and the modern, backbeat-heavy sound of rhythm and blues.[35] Like some of his peers, he may have attended blues venues only on nights designated for exclusively white audiences—a necessity in the segregated South.[36] Many of his future recordings were inspired by local African-American musicians such as Arthur Crudup and Rufus Thomas.[37][38] B.B. King recalled that he had known Presley before he was popular when they both used to frequent Beale Street.[39] By the time he graduated from high school in June 1953, Presley had already singled out music as his future.[40][41]

</fragment>

At the Country Disc Jockey Convention in early November, Presley was voted the year's most promising male artist.[79] Several record companies had by now shown interest in signing him. Songwriters were obliged to forgo one-third of their customary royalties in exchange for having Presley perform their compositions.[82][b] By December, RCA had begun to heavily promote its new singer, and before month's end had reissued many of his Sun recordings.[85]
